name: Jacob Steeves
title: RT by @const_reborn: NOVA Blueprint: 678.5 Billion Possible Molecules Last week, we upgraded Blueprint to Boltz-2-based scoring. This week, we're expanding the chemical search space by more than 11×. Reactions: 5 → 44 Building blocks: 225K → 2.03M Enumerable chemical space: 61.1B → 678.5B molecules The implications are bigger than the numbers. Blueprint competitors now have to find the highest-scoring set within an 11× larger chemical space, using a substantially more computationally intensive scoring model than before. That makes deciding where to search and which molecules are worth spending inference on more important than ever. That's the problem Blueprint is designed to optimize: developing increasingly efficient and generalizable algorithms for navigating ultra-large chemical spaces. Winning algorithms must outperform the incumbent across four different targets. By repeatedly changing the target, Blueprint applies evolutionary pressure toward search strategies that generalize rather than overfit to develop code that can more reliably screen chemical space for new unseen targets. The expansion incorporates the SANQI reaction space alongside broader molecular validity and filtering rules covering physicochemical properties, ring structure, elemental composition, molecular complexity, and other structural constraints. We're also upgrading how Blueprint rewards diversity. Submission entropy will now be calculated using atom-pair fingerprints rather than MACCS keys, with the threshold moving to 0.35. The expanded reaction and building-block database underlying the new 678.5B search space is available openly on HF. Competition open to all. https://huggingface.co/datasets/Metanova/Mol-Rxn-DB/tree/sanqi

name: Joseph Jacks
title: Doing AI at scale is not just a question of how many parameters a model has. It is how much hardware and energy we need to store those parameters, move them around, and repeatedly compute with them. At 4–16-bit precision, each weight alone requires roughly 4–16 DRAM storage transistors, before adding the arithmetic, caches, interconnects, and other machinery needed to run inference. 🌱 … Biology raises a much more interesting question: are we counting at the right level? A tubulin dimer contains eight tryptophan residues, whose indole chromophores form networks with experimentally observed fluorescence enhancement consistent with collective optical behavior.. Which gives us a concrete physical substrate to investigate beneath the familiar neuron-and-synapse picture. Here is the scale that fascinates me.. A rough upper-scale brain protein fermi estimate suggests around 500 quintillion tubulin-associated tryptophan sites. If each indole acts as a useful switching unit, and we use 100–1,000 trillion synapses as a deliberately coarse parameter proxy, that is roughly 500,000–5 million candidate molecular switching units per “parameter”. This suggests that comparing AI parameters with synapses may miss an enormous amount of underlying machinery. The exciting question is whether that machinery contributes independently usable computation and learning. I believe it does. And I propose that we should measure and introduce its scaling laws, rather than assume today’s neural-network scaling laws tell us what biology can do.
